text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Already in 1995 it would have been clear to the defence department that Volvo Aero's operations in Arboga would have to be shut down, sources told the newspaper. Outgoing Defence Minister Thage Peterson addressed questions on television about the government's role in the events on Thursday. In a parliamentary debate on Thursday Peterson said he would try to ensure the the company's civil operations would stay.

- All during the autumn Volvo's board debated about the replacement for managing director Soren Gyll who said this week he would retire. Other candidates included deputy managing director Lennart Jeansson, SKF head Peter Augustsson who was formerly the head of Volvo Car. Finally Volvo board head Bert-Olof Svanholm's favourite candidate, the head of appliance maker Electrolux, got the job.

- The effect of Prime Minister Goran Persson's plan to spend 10 billion crowns of a forecast budget surplus on public finances instead of paying back the state debt has not had as dramatic an effect as people say. The Swedish debt market has weakened with a general trend internationally since his proposal was announced.

- Clothing retailer Hennes & Mauritz had another record financial year 1995/1996, posting a 44 percent increase in pre-tax profits at 1.91 billion crowns and a five-for-one share split. Managing Director Stefan Persson says he is optimistic, but he doesn't expect people to change their buying habits drastically in 1997. Because of unemployment and budget cutbacks, many Swedes have cut down on spending.

- The EMU debate is splitting the government. Swedish Interior Minister Jorgen Andersson says he supports linking the Swedish crown to the European Union's monetary union (EMU) from its planned 1999 start, but says this would be impossible given current public support. Education & Science Minister Carl Tham has announced recently that he is completely against it.
- Some 1,800 small, fast growing companies have doubled their turnover in the past four years, creating 36,000 jobs and increased their sales by 220 billion crowns.
- With a budget of 300 million crowns Sweden's tourist board plans to double the number of tourists coming to Sweden and create 25,000 jobs.
- Cooperation between Finnair and Denmark's Maersk Air on the profitable Copenhagen-Stockholm route will mean losses for Scandinavian Airline SAS.
- Police have compiled a list of some 90 foreign firms who have been accused of swindling Swedish businessmen.
